The story features subtle, character-driven revelations that are both surprising to the reader and entirely appropriate within the context of the narrative. 

First, in the cave, Marta reveals that her flight isn't actually on Friday, as she had led everyone to believe, giving them four extra days together. This is surprising because the story has built a bittersweet tension around their imminent departure, yet it is completely appropriate for Marta's character, as it was established earlier that she constantly invents stories and histories (telling people Friday simply because it "sounded decisive"). 

Second, at the café, Marta reveals the truth about her late-night habits. From the very first paragraph, the reader is led to believe through Ines's perspective that Marta's lamp is on until 3:00 a.m. because she is passionately writing. When Marta confesses that she actually has insomnia and sits at her desk looking at Ines's dark window to find the peace to try sleeping again, it subverts the central image of the story in a surprising way. However, it feels entirely earned and appropriate given the quiet, mutual pining and "managing" of unspoken feelings the two women have been doing all month.
